items.originalTitle: Here’s where you can save (a little) on the Ocarina of Time remake
items.author: Cameron Faulkner
items.title: Here’s where you can save (a little) on the Ocarina of Time remake
items.summary: The Nintendo Switch 2 remake delivers a complete graphical overhaul and numerous quality-of-life updates to the ‘98 classic. | Image: Nintendo A lot of people have The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo Switch 2 on their holiday wishlist. In case you haven’t bought it yet, I wanted to share some small but welcome deals happening on the physical and digital versions of the game. Costco members can currently grab the cartridge edition for $62.99, down from its regular price of $69.99 (it’s the only retailer currently discounting the physical version). Both Amazon and Costco are also selling the digital version for $54.99, a small $5 discount. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Where to Buy: $59.99 $54.99 at Amazon (Digital) $69.99 $62.99 at Costco (Physical) Ocarina of Time is one of Nintendo’s most groundbreaking titles, having served as its first 3D Zelda game when it launched in 1998. Parts of the original game haven’t aged particularly well — namely some dungeon design and the game’s tricky 3D navigation, since there was only one analog stick at the time — which makes it tough for some to enjoy going back to play the N64 version. Thankfully, the Switch 2 remake introduces several fixes, a host of quality-of-life improvements, and, of course, some lovely visuals that make it a graphics powerhouse by today’s standards. If you go the digital route, a recent Switch 2 update lets you gift games to players in your family group. It doesn’t have to be your actual family, either, just up to eight people you designate as part of your group. The digital game will then appear gift-wrapped on their homescreen. Read our full Ocarina of Time review .

items.originalTitle: I’m an AI leader at a tech giant. Our industry has stopped taking safety seriously | Anonymous
items.author: Anonymous
items.title: I’m an AI leader at a tech giant. Our industry has stopped taking safety seriously | Anonymous
items.summary: We’re developing the most powerful tech in history – but trust, safeguarding and privacy are being sidelined in favour of huge profit I’m a senior AI leader at one of the world’s biggest tech companies, and the products we put out into the world are increasingly being recklessly rushed, without proper consideration. The tech industry used to take safety and privacy seriously, but lately I have become worried by how rash we have become. In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford. If you want to properly understand the actions of big tech, you have to look at the industry’s culture. It moves fast and there is a mindset of constant one-upmanship. Being first matters financially. But just as importantly, competition is believed to bring out the best in people. The writer is an AI expert working in the tech industry. A version of this piece originally appeared with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism as part of its Secret Source series, a regular column featuring industry whistleblowers

items.originalTitle: I’m not interested in having sex with near strangers. As a newly single man, how do I navigate dating? | Leading questions
items.author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith
items.title: I’m not interested in having sex with near strangers. As a newly single man, how do I navigate dating? | Leading questions
items.summary: You don’t have to have sex because it’s ‘what’s expected’, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. But you may want to be explicit about what you do want Read more Leading questions How do I navigate being single when I’m not interested in sex with near strangers? I don’t judge anyone, consenting adults can do whatever they like – but for me, sex has to come with trust and, frankly, love, or at least the potential of love. I’m recently single after a long and toxic relationship, and I’ve never dated – I got on the dating scene and found that if I don’t try to get in someone’s pants by the third date, no matter how much of a nice time we’re having, they disappear – and in fact I’ve had some women do the old “call yourself a man” at me, in one memorable case, after they specifically said “not tonight” and I said “no problem” (the response was a frustrated “don’t you have needs?!”). I’ve tried to go along with it and do what’s expected but I don’t enjoy it, it just feels a bit wrong, and when I’ve done this it kills the vibe we had, probably because I can’t get into it properly. I’ve always been into the person, not just the body, but it takes time to get to know someone enough to feel comfortable being intimate. So how can I keep a nice relationship going, so that I can develop the trust I need for sex, without them losing interest because I’m not doing (what I assume) everyone else on the dating scene is doing?

items.originalTitle: Lumière album review – finding solace in the rich, lyrical world of French cello music
items.author: Erica Jeal
items.title: Lumière album review – finding solace in the rich, lyrical world of French cello music
items.summary: Laura van der Heijden/Jâms Coleman (Chandos) The piano-cello duo explore the consoling beauty of works by Franck, Fauré and Mel Bonis, with a welcome rediscovery among the highlights This is the third release from the team of cellist Laura van der Heijden and pianist Jâms Coleman . They say it grew from a desire to record “music of consolation and warmth”, and every piece on this all-French programme fits the bill. The most substantial is Franck’s 1886 Sonata, best known in its original, violin-and-piano version but also claimed by cellists ever since the composer sanctioned an arrangement not long after its premiere. It gets a persuasively expansive performance here. Coleman’s piano is unfailingly clear and detailed; van der Heijden’s playing is angry and urgent in the second movement, impassioned in the climactic passages of the finale. More generally, though, her melodies spool out in endless lines, her tone rich and sustained, her phrasing unbroken almost to a fault: just occasionally the cello line feels as if it could use more breath, more space in which to ask questions. There’s a sense of security in that sustained tone, though, and it serves the consolatory aspect of the programme well. Massenet’s Méditation from Thaïs and Fauré’s bittersweet Sicilienne are the most familiar of the shorter pieces; alongside these there are a transcription of Paix, a melancholy yet consolatory song by Charlotte Sohy; the compact and characterful Three Pieces by Nadia Boulanger; and a characteristically lovely Élégie by the still-underrated Darius Milhaud. And from Franck’s protege Mel Bonis we hear the 1904 Cello Sonata, a searching work that manages to feel tautly argued and rhapsodic at the same time – a worthwhile rediscovery.

items.originalTitle: The best reds and whites from the golden state: our pick of Californian wines
items.author: Mina Holland
items.title: The best reds and whites from the golden state: our pick of Californian wines
items.summary: Having built its reputation on big, brash reds, the centre of US winemaking is keeping pace with changing tastes and now becoming known for crisp whites, too I was always more of a Dawson’s Creek girlie than a fan of The OC , yet the subject of this column has found me wrestling with the earworm that is the latter’s theme tune : “California, here we come/Right back where we started from.” For Scribe Winery , at the southern end of the Sonoma Valley, this is apt, though I’m not sure winemaker Andrew Mariani would thank me for the comparison. Since buying 100 hectares here in 2007, he and his brother, Adam, have been restoring the land to viticulture after an interlude as a turkey farm. Some of the Marianis’ vines are riesling and sylvaner, honouring the German immigrant family who first cultivated them here in the 1850s, but they make up a small proportion of Scribe’s production, which is focused on bright, bracing chardonnay and terroir-driven pinot noir. It’s an approach that reflects the trend of drinkers turning away from the beefy reds, particularly cabernet sauvignon, that made California famous, towards fresher – dare I say Old World? – styles. Andrew has pulled up “cab” on recently acquired land to make room for more pinot, and his chardonnays see no oak, which has long been associated with California whites. Some even go into keg, making them more accessible.
